question: Describe a time you worked with a cross-functional or diverse team to achieve a shared goal. What was your specific contribution?

raiseTranscript.text: On my first internship, our product team had engineering, design, and marketing all trying to launch a new onboarding flow. I owned the A/B test setup and made sure the data pipeline was ready before design finalized the mocks.
What specifically did you do when the marketing timeline slipped?
I flagged the dependency in our standup, offered to shift my test window by two days, and checked in daily with the marketing lead so we still hit the launch date.

raiseNotes: Q: cross-functional team shared goal contribution
Internship onboarding flow launch with eng/design/marketing
Owned A/B test setup and data pipeline readiness
Flagged marketing slip, shifted own window, daily check-ins
Quote: 'I checked in daily so we still hit the date'
Follow-up: handled slip by adjusting own work and communicating
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for junior. The candidate described owning a concrete piece of work inside a cross-functional launch and adjusting their own timeline when another team slipped. The quote about daily check-ins shows proactive coordination rather than waiting for direction. This matches the level expectation of individual ownership plus coachability. The story stays local but demonstrates learning how to unblock a shared goal. Biggest strength is the clear link between their action and keeping the launch on track.

lowerTranscript.text: We had a team project with people from different departments. I mostly did the tasks my manager assigned me and waited for updates in meetings.
How did you handle any misalignment between teams?
I just did my part and let the leads sort it out.

lowerNotes: Q: cross-functional team shared goal contribution
Vague team project, no specific outcome mentioned
Did assigned tasks and waited for updates
When asked about misalignment: 'let the leads sort it out'
Follow-up: no evidence of proactive coordination or adjustment
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for junior. The answer stays at the level of completing assigned tasks without showing any initiative to connect across functions. The follow-up response reveals passive behavior when misalignment occurred. At junior level we look for ownership of one's own work and willingness to adjust or communicate; neither appears here. The story lacks a concrete goal or measurable contribution. Biggest gap is absence of any action that helped the shared outcome.

raiseTranscript.text: Last year I drove a pricing experiment that needed data science, finance, and two product teams. I mapped the data requirements, ran weekly syncs, and created a shared dashboard so everyone saw the same numbers.
What happened when finance pushed back on the methodology?
I scheduled a 30-minute working session, walked through their concerns with sample data, and adjusted the test design so finance could sign off without delaying the launch.

raiseNotes: Q: cross-functional team shared goal contribution
Pricing experiment across data science, finance, two product teams
Mapped requirements, weekly syncs, shared dashboard
Handled finance pushback with working session and adjusted design
Quote: 'adjusted the test design so finance could sign off'
Follow-up: used direct collaboration to resolve conflict
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for senior. The candidate shows influence without authority by creating shared visibility and resolving a cross-team blocker through a targeted working session. The outcome of getting finance sign-off demonstrates impact beyond their immediate team. This aligns with senior expectations of driving results across functions. The story includes a clear metric (launch not delayed) tied to their actions. Biggest strength is the proactive resolution of disagreement rather than escalation.

lowerTranscript.text: I worked with several teams on a feature rollout. I attended the meetings and provided updates when asked.
How did you resolve differing priorities?
I raised it in the meeting and hoped the PM would decide.

lowerNotes: Q: cross-functional team shared goal contribution
Feature rollout with multiple teams, no specific outcome
Attended meetings and gave updates on request
On differing priorities: 'hoped the PM would decide'
Follow-up: no evidence of influence or problem-solving
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for senior. The candidate describes passive participation rather than driving cross-team alignment. At senior level we expect evidence of influence without authority and measurable impact; the story contains neither. The follow-up response shows reliance on others to resolve conflict. The contribution remains limited to attending meetings. Biggest gap is lack of any action that moved the shared goal forward.

raiseTranscript.text: My team needed to integrate a new partner API while also supporting two internal platform teams. I assigned clear owners, ran bi-weekly joint demos, and coached two engineers on how to negotiate scope with the partner.
What did you do when one engineer kept missing deadlines?
I had a direct conversation, identified the root cause was unclear requirements, paired them with a platform engineer for two sprints, and the deliverables landed on time.

raiseNotes: Q: cross-functional team shared goal contribution
Partner API integration with internal platform teams
Assigned owners, joint demos, coached negotiation skills
Handled underperformance via root-cause conversation and pairing
Quote: 'paired them with a platform engineer for two sprints'
Follow-up: addressed underperformance and created leverage
manager.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for manager. The candidate shows how they created leverage through joint rituals and skill coaching while directly addressing underperformance. The pairing action produced an on-time delivery and developed the engineer. This matches manager expectations of owning team outcomes and developing people. The story demonstrates both process and people leadership. Biggest strength is the concrete handling of performance issues inside a cross-team effort.

lowerTranscript.text: I coordinated between my team and two partner teams on a migration. I made sure everyone had the status updates.
How did you handle team members who were not aligned?
I sent more emails and hoped it would improve.

lowerNotes: Q: cross-functional team shared goal contribution
Migration across teams, no outcome or metric stated
Provided status updates
On misalignment: sent more emails
Follow-up: no direct coaching or performance management
manager.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for manager. The answer focuses on status reporting rather than creating team leverage or addressing performance. Manager level requires evidence of developing people and handling underperformance; the follow-up shows avoidance. The story lacks any example of coaching or outcome ownership. Biggest gap is treating coordination as communication instead of active leadership.

raiseTranscript.text: We had to unify three acquired companies' billing systems into one platform. I set the north-star metric, created a cross-org steering group, and made trade-off decisions on which legacy features to sunset to hit the 18-month target.
How did you manage resistance from the acquired teams?
I visited each site, listened to their concerns in person, then adjusted the migration sequence so each team saw early wins while still protecting the overall timeline.

raiseNotes: Q: cross-functional team shared goal contribution
Unified billing across three acquired companies
Set north-star metric, steering group, made sunset trade-offs
Handled resistance by site visits and adjusted sequence for early wins
Quote: 'adjusted the migration sequence so each team saw early wins'
Follow-up: strategic judgment on org-level trade-offs
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for exec. The candidate demonstrates strategic judgment by defining a north-star metric and making explicit trade-offs across acquired entities. The site visits and sequence adjustment show long-term thinking about change management at org scale. This fits exec expectations of high ambiguity and business-level impact. The 18-month target provides a clear outcome anchor. Biggest strength is balancing local concerns with the overall integration goal.

lowerTranscript.text: I sponsored a company-wide initiative to improve collaboration across regions. I asked leaders to share updates in the all-hands.
What trade-offs did you make when priorities conflicted?
I let each region decide and tried to stay neutral.

lowerNotes: Q: cross-functional team shared goal contribution
Sponsored collaboration initiative, no specific business outcome
Asked leaders to share updates
On trade-offs: 'let each region decide'
Follow-up: no evidence of strategic decisions or leverage
exec.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for exec. The answer shows sponsorship without strategic ownership or trade-off decisions. At exec level we look for org-level impact and willingness to make hard calls; the follow-up reveals avoidance. The story lacks any measurable result or long-term thinking. Biggest gap is treating the role as passive oversight instead of active direction.

diagnostic.junior: Individual task ownership inside one project
diagnostic.senior: Cross-team coordination with measurable launch impact
diagnostic.manager: Team leverage plus direct performance coaching
